32.title: Architecture
32.text:
Architecture
PocketMageOS is a single-core-visible cooperative state machine on an ESP32-S3. One variable, CurrentAppState, decides which app owns the keyboard and the screens; the main loop routes every keystroke and every screen refresh to that app’s handlers. This page is the map of the whole system and where each part is documented in depth.
The layers
flowchart TB
    subgraph APPS["Apps"]
        direction LR
        A1["native apps<br>src/OS_APPS/"]
        A2["ELF apps<br>SD card"]
    end
    subgraph RUNTIME["PocketMageOS runtime"]
        R1["boot, dispatch, state, timeout, app loading<br>PocketMageV3.cpp, UTILS.cpp, elf_runner.cpp"]
    end
    subgraph LIB["PocketMage Library - the SDK (lib/PocketMage_SDK/)"]
        L1["OLED, E-Ink, SD, keyboard, touch, clock, buzzer,<br>WiFi, fonts, layout, UI, i18n"]
    end
    subgraph HW["Hardware (ESP32-S3)"]
        H1["E-Ink, OLED, TCA8418 keyboard, MPR121 touch,<br>PCF8563 RTC, buzzer, microSD, USB, radios"]
    end
    APPS --> RUNTIME --> LIB --> HW

Apps never touch hardware directly. They call the library; the library is the only layer that knows the pins. That boundary is what lets the same app code build as a native app, as a loadable ELF, and against future hardware revisions.
Boot
On power-up the OS mounts the SD card, initializes the displays and keyboard, and loads persistent settings from NVS. It then decides which app to enter based on how the device woke:

Normal boot enters HOME, unless HOME_ON_BOOT is off.
A wake with a held shortcut key enters the mapped app (for example n opens TXT). The mapping is bootShortcutApp() in UTILS.cpp.
A wake from now-later returns to the app that was active before sleep, with its saved state restored.

Dispatch
The main loop in PocketMageV3.cpp is a cooperative dispatcher. Two functions switch on CurrentAppState:

processKB() routes each keypress to the active app’s keyboard handler.
applicationEinkHandler() routes each screen refresh to the active app’s draw handler.

Every app is three functions - init, handle input, draw - and the app never drives the loop itself.
flowchart LR
    KB["keypress"] --> PKB["processKB()"]
    RF["refresh tick"] --> AEH["applicationEinkHandler()"]
    PKB --> SW{"switch<br>CurrentAppState"}
    AEH --> SW
    SW --> H["HOME"]
    SW --> T["TXT"]
    SW --> F["FILEWIZ"]
    SW --> E["other apps..."]
    H --> HND["active app's<br>input + draw handlers"]
    T --> HND
    F --> HND
    E --> HND

The full state model, the AppState enum, the HOME sub-states, and the transition helpers are in the System State reference.
The two displays
The device pairs a slow, sharp 320x240 E-Ink panel with a fast 256x32 OLED. Anything that benefits from instant feedback - prompts, status, timers - goes to the OLED; anything that benefits from a large readable page - notes, files, calendars - goes to the E-Ink. The E-Ink panel is guarded by a recursive mutex and refreshed from a background task, so code in other tasks must respect that boundary. The display APIs are in the PocketMage Library reference, with the full per-module contract on the SDK API docs.
State and timeout
The OS keeps shared runtime state in globals.h: the active app, the home sub-state, the re-init flag, persistent preferences, the active filesystem handle, and the idle-timeout lockout. After IDLE_TIME without input the OS shows the idle state; after TIMEOUT it sleeps. Apps reset the idle clock with resetIdle() or hold it off with disableTimeout. The full list is in the System State reference.
Storage
Files live on a microSD card, reached through the library’s SD module (PM_SD()). The OS tracks a working file and an editing file for save/load flows, and installed ELF apps live in four slots under /apps/slot1 through /apps/slot4, tracked in NVS as ELFINFO1 through ELFINFO4.
The SD gateway owns file I/O. Streams, directory cursors, and the snapshot are scoped to
their calling task; app exit closes that task’s resources after callbacks finish.
The base ELF stream closes after relocation, and overlays use logical handles
with short-lived reads. USB transfer claims exclusive card access only after
audio and HID shutdown and a successful FAT unmount. The card is not unmounted
or put to sleep while a directory is still open.
Wi-Fi setup at boot does not create the Wi-Fi worker task or its 10,240-byte
stack. The first enable() creates them, and stop() frees them again.
Shared audio and USB
Native and ELF apps share the SDK’s audio, media, drawing, and idle services.
Generated C wrappers preserve the ABI 2 boundary; compatibility adapters retain
legacy signatures. Metadata parsing, PCM gain/timing, and NVS audio preferences
live in the SDK rather than in PocketM

44.title: Build Environments & PlatformIO Setup
44.text:
Build Environments & PlatformIO Setup
PocketMage firmware is built with PlatformIO. The build configuration lives in Code/PocketMageOS/platformio.ini and defines two environments that produce the firmware variants. Third-party apps are not built in this tree; they are compiled against the PocketMage SDK (see ELF Apps).
The two build environments



Environment
Target
Purpose




PM_PRODUCTION
Production hardware (N16R2, Quad PSRAM enabled)
The stable OS image flashed to production devices


PM_BETA
Beta hardware (N16R8, PSRAM forced disabled)
A test build with the latest changes



The two environments share a common [common] section and differ in hardware target and version string.
Running pio run with no arguments builds both defaults (PM_PRODUCTION and PM_BETA). Build one explicitly with pio run -e <name>.
Prerequisites

VS Code installed
Python 3 installed
PlatformIO Core (installed automatically by the VS Code extension, or via pip install platformio)
The PocketMage source code, cloned from GitHub

The ESP32 platform support downloads automatically on the first build, so the first build is noticeably slower.
Setup
Linux

Install python3-venv if it is missing:
sudo apt install python3-venv


Install the PlatformIO IDE extension in VS Code.

Open the PocketMage source folder in VS Code.

When PlatformIO asks for a project folder, choose Code/PocketMageOS/.

Build from the PlatformIO toolbar or the command palette.


macOS
Use the same steps as Linux. No extra setup is required.
Windows

Install Git to clone the repository.
Follow the same PlatformIO IDE steps as Linux.
Build from the PlatformIO toolbar in VS Code.

Command line
From Code/PocketMageOS/:
pio run -e PM_PRODUCTION   # production firmware
pio run -e PM_BETA         # beta firmware

ELF apps
Third-party apps are not built with this environment set. They are compiled against the PocketMage SDK into .app.elf files, packaged with an icon as a .tar, and installed through the app loader. See ELF Apps and the app loader section of the command manual.
Testing
Run the hardware-independent firmware tests from Code/PocketMageOS with Python 3
and a C++ compiler supporting AddressSanitizer and UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer:
python3 -m unittest discover -s tests/host -p 'test_*.py'

CI builds PM_PRODUCTION and PM_BETA on every push. Verify hardware behavior on
the device; see Crash logs for reading crash reports after a reboot.

56.title: Crash logs
56.text:
Crash logs
When PocketMageOS crashes, it keeps a short record of the crash in memory that
survives a reboot. After the device starts again, it saves that record to the SD
card as a text report. Both firmware environments have this turned on.
Retrieve a report

Flash the firmware and keep its exact firmware.elf and firmware.bin
together. Rebuilding can change code addresses.
Reproduce the failure with a writable SD card installed.
Let the device reboot and finish starting up without removing power.
Copy /logs/crash/crash-*.txt from the card, either through USB file transfer or
by reading the card on a computer.

The filename is crash-<boot nonce>-<record CRC>.txt. The serial log’s CRASH tag
prints Saved /logs/crash/... when the report is written. If saving fails, the report
stays pending and the OS tries again every five seconds. If no card was mounted at
boot, insert one and restart without removing power; inserting a card alone does
not mount it.
You can also read the report over serial. Unplug any USB accessory, connect a
computer and open the serial monitor at 115200 baud. The report is sent each time
a USB serial connection is detected, so reconnect the cable if you opened the
monitor after the device was already connected.
What is captured

The panic reason, and the message from abort() or a failed assertion.
The core, the current task name, the fault PC and up to 60 backtrace PCs.
The Xtensa registers (A0-A15, PS, SAR, EXCCAUSE, EXCVADDR, LBEG, LEND, LCOUNT)
when an exception frame is available.
The firmware’s ELF SHA256 and the uptime in milliseconds.
A snapshot of the OS taken by the main loop shortly before the crash: the
active app, whether an ELF app was running, which feature owned the USB port,
the free, largest and lowest-ever internal heap, and the number of tasks. The
report shows how old the snapshot is.
The last 1 KB of SDK log lines, under Recent log:. These come from the
logger’s memory, so they are there even when logging to a file is off. See
Logging
for the line format.

Decode firmware addresses
Use the exact ELF from the flashed build. Check that its SHA256 matches the
report’s Firmware ELF SHA256 line:
shasum -a 256 firmware.elf

From the directory containing that ELF, run:
"$HOME/.platformio/packages/toolchain-xtensa-esp-elf/bin/xtensa-esp32s3-elf-addr2line" \
  -aipfC -e firmware.elf

Paste the addresses from the report’s Backtrace PCs: line, then press Ctrl-D.
The tool prints the function and source line for each address. If the backtrace is
corrupt, the report’s PC line is still useful. EXCVADDR is the address that was
accessed, not a code address.
The firmware ELF only covers the OS, the SDK and the USB driver. Addresses inside
an ELF app need that app’s own build files, so keep them with the report.
How it works
src/diagnostics/crash_log.cpp hooks Arduino’s panic handler before
PocketMage_INIT() runs, using the -Wl,--wrap=esp_panic_handler linker flag. At
crash time it only copies data into RTC memory that survives a reboot. It does not
touch the SD card, serial or the heap.
After the next boot, pm_crash::poll() writes the report to a temporary file,
reads it back to check it, and renames it to .txt. A report is never written
over an existing file. Saving waits while the card is in USB file transfer mode.
Only the latest crash is kept in memory; saved reports pile up on the card. A
power loss, a brownout or a device that hangs without crashing leaves no report.
This is a crash summary, not a full core dump.
Build and test
From Code/PocketMageOS:
pio run -e PM_BETA -j 2
python3 -m unittest discover -s tests/host -p test_crash_log.py

Use PM_PRODUCTION for production hardware. The tests need a C++17 compiler with
AddressSanitizer and UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer. They run the real capture and
report code against simulated hardware, so check a real crash report to confirm
behavior on the device.

63.title: PocketMageOS
63.text:
PocketMageOS
PocketMageOS is the operating system layer of the firmware. It boots the device, starts and switches apps, routes keyboard input, dispatches screen updates, and tracks the system state that every app depends on. This page explains how that runtime works and where the code lives.




  

Boot and routeStarts the right app, routes keyboard input, and keeps screen updates on the right handler.




  
  

Manage stateTracks timeout, sleep, lock, and the active app.




  
  
  
  
  
  
  
  
  
  
  
  
  
  

Bridge hardwareCoordinates the shared hardware layer, storage, and device helpers.




  
  
  

Support appsNative apps and ELF apps plug into the same runtime model.


The app runtime model
Every PocketMage app is a set of three functions. The OS calls them at the right time; the app never drives the loop itself.

*_INIT() - runs once when the app is entered. Sets app state and prepares the screen.
processKB_*() - runs on every keypress. The app reads the key, updates its state, and queues a redraw.
einkHandler_*() - runs when the screen needs updating. The app draws the current state to the E-Ink buffer.

The dispatch loop in PocketMageV3.cpp owns the switch between these handlers. It is a switch (CurrentAppState) that routes each keystroke and each E-Ink refresh to the active app. Adding an app means adding a case to that switch and an entry to the AppState enum in globals.h. The spots are marked // ADD APP CASES HERE.
How boot works
On power-up, PocketMageOS mounts the SD card, initializes the displays and keyboard, and loads persistent settings from NVS. It then checks which app to enter. This depends on how the device was woken:

Normal boot - enters the home app (unless the HOME_ON_BOOT setting is off).
Woken from sleep with a shortcut key - enters the app mapped to that key. For example, pressing N while sleeping opens TXT. The mapping is bootShortcutApp() in UTILS.cpp.
Woken from now-later - returns to the app that was active before sleep, restoring its saved state.

State the OS tracks
The OS keeps shared runtime state in globals.h. The pieces you will meet most often:

CurrentAppState - which app is active. This drives the dispatch switch.
CurrentHOMEState - the home screen mode (HOME_HOME or NOWLATER).
newState - a flag that tells the loop to re-run *_INIT() for the target app.
disableTimeout - a global lockout so an app can prevent idle sleep while it is busy.
prefs - persistent preferences stored in NVS.
global_fs - the active filesystem handle.

The timeout system is also part of the OS. After IDLE_TIME without input, the OS shows the mage idle state; after TIMEOUT seconds it sleeps. Apps can reset the idle clock with resetIdle() or block it entirely with disableTimeout.
How apps reach the hardware
Apps do not talk to hardware directly. They call the PocketMage Library, which owns the physical devices. OLED().sysMessage(...) flashes a message, EINK().refresh() pushes the E-Ink buffer, KB() handles key state, and SD() handles storage. The library is the only layer that knows the pins. This is what lets the same app code build for native, ELF, and future hardware revisions.
See PocketMage Library for the full module map.
Native vs ELF apps

Native apps live in src/OS_APPS/, are compiled into the firmware, and are wired into the dispatch switch.
ELF apps are compiled separately against the PocketMage SDK into a .app.elf, packed with an overlay sidecar, and loaded from the SD card at runtime through the app loader. No firmware reflash is involved. The runner (src/elf_runner.cpp) relocates the base image with esp_elf, then pages the app’s code into executable RAM through the elf_overlay runtime, and runs the app’s entry in its own task while the OS loop stands down.

Both follow the same three-function shape. The difference is where the code ships and how it is loaded. See ELF Apps for the device side, Making Apps for the workflow, and the SDK docs for the binary contract.
Source layout

Code/PocketMageOS/src/PocketMageV3.cpp - main loop and app dispatch
Code/PocketMageOS/src/OS_APPS/ - native app code, one file per app
Code/PocketMageOS/src/UTILS.cpp - shared prompts, boot shortcuts, and runtime helpers
Code/PocketMageOS/include/globals.h - app prototypes, app state, shared runtime state
Code/PocketMageOS/include/config.h - pins and system settings
Code/PocketMageOS/lib/PocketMage_SDK/ - the reusable hardware layer (the PocketMage SDK, vendored as a submodule)
Code/PocketMageOS/lib/elf_overlay/ - the overlay runtime that pages ELF-app code into executable RAM
Code/PocketMageOS/src/elf_runner.cpp - loads and runs installed ELF apps
Code/PocketMageOS/src/diagnostics/ - retained panic capture and post-reboot crash reports

72.text:
PocketMage FAQ
Helpful links

PocketMage.org
PocketMage on GitHub
PocketMage on Discord
Ashtf on YouTube
Ashtf on Patreon

General information
What is PocketMage?
PocketMage is a hackable, open-source PDA focused on productivity. Use it to take notes, keep track of tasks, journal, schedule your week, and more. It is a clamshell design with a clear shell, a full tactile thumb keyboard, a large E-Ink main display, and a smaller OLED secondary display. All hardware and software is open source, which makes it ideal for hacking and add-ons.
How much is the kit?
The final production kit is not released yet and the price is not final. The target is around $150 for a full kit.
How hard is it to build the kit?
The kit is designed so anyone can build it. The only tool you need is one allen key, and there is no soldering, programming, or electronics involved in the build process.
Will I be able to get PocketMage if I live outside the USA?
Yes. We plan to ship worldwide.
When can I order?
There is no set release date yet. Once the beta production run is complete and the software matures, we will move to final production.
How can I get notified when the kit releases?
Visit PocketMage.org and click the “Join the Mailing List!” button.
How can I keep up with the project?
Subscribe to Ashtf’s YouTube channel for video updates, Ashtf’s Patreon for exclusive weekly written updates, and the PocketMage Discord server for community updates.
Building and operating the PocketMage
Where is the build guide?
The video build guide is here.
Is there a guide on the key operations?
Yes. Use the Command Manual.
How do I flash the firmware?

Carefully remove the battery (pull on the plastic connector).
Ensure the DIP switch for programming mode is ON.
Hold the power button while plugging the PocketMage into your computer. Nothing should happen.
Open The Web Flasher in a Chrome-based browser and select your firmware version. The most recent stable build is recommended.
If you want to keep your saved settings, check the “Preserve user data during installation” box.
Hit the flash button and select the PocketMage from the list of USB devices.
When flashing is done, unplug the PocketMage and re-insert the battery.

PocketMage should boot up automatically.
What SD card can I use?
Use a microSD card formatted as FAT32 with an MBR partition table. Cards up to 32 GB are recommended; 8 GB is a good sweet spot because PocketMage files are small. The smaller the card, the faster the device. Cards larger than 32 GB must be explicitly forced to FAT32 + MBR and are not recommended. See Format a MicroSD Card for the exact steps.
Where are the CAD files?
CAD files are available only to beta testers until the final production release. If you are a beta tester, find the password-protected archive here and the password in the beta Discord channel.
Where can I get an extra battery?
International kits do not come with a battery because of shipping regulations. Battery links for common countries are here.
What is the programming mode switch?
The programming mode switch connects the USB port directly to the microcontroller, bypassing the USB and battery charge controller. You can keep it on and use the device normally, but charging is limited to 500 mA instead of fast charging.
Build and app docs
For the current setup path, start here:

Build Environments
App API Reference
System State Reference

Common issues
My dictionary isn’t working
The English dictionary is not installed out of the box and must be downloaded to the SD card. Find the dictionary files here. Connect the PocketMage to your computer with the USB app and drop all the .txt files into the dictionary folder.
I can’t flash the firmware
Ensure the battery is unplugged and the programming mode DIP switch is ON. See the flashing guide above.
My SD card isn’t working
First, ensure the card is 32 GB or smaller (8 GB is recommended). Next, ensure it is formatted as FAT32 with an MBR partition table. It will not work otherwise. See Format a MicroSD Card.
I found a software bug
Report the bug in detail on the GitHub issues page, including steps to reproduce.

97.text:
Features
PocketMage is a productivity PDA first. The device focuses on reading, editing, quick navigation, and simple workflows that fit E-Ink. This page covers what the current firmware can do and what is planned.

109.title: What is PocketMage?
109.text:
What is PocketMage?
PocketMage is a clamshell PDA built around an ESP32-S3. It is open-source hardware and software, designed to be built at home, hacked, and extended. This page explains the device and the two software layers that run on it.




  
  
  

Dual displaysA 320x240 E-Ink panel for the main workspace and a 256x32 OLED for status and fast feedback.




  
  
  
  
  
  
  
  
  

Full keyboardA tactile thumb keyboard with four layers: normal, shift, function, and function plus shift.




  
  
  

Two software layersPocketMageOS handles apps and state; the PocketMage Library handles the hardware.




  

Open and extendableBuild apps with C++ or run Wrench scripts from the terminal. Load third-party apps at runtime.


The hardware
The main display is a 3.1" 1-bit E-Ink panel (320x240). E-Ink is sharp and power efficient, but slow to update, so a small OLED sits below it for status text, prompts, and feedback that needs to appear instantly. The keyboard is a matrix driven by a TCA8418 IC, which is why it can support four separate key layers.
The device runs on an ESP32-S3 with 16 MB flash and WiFi and Bluetooth radios. Storage lives on a microSD card. Everything else - RTC, buzzer, battery management, USB, and an expansion port with I2C/SPI/UART breakouts - is exposed to software through the shared library.
The two software layers
PocketMage firmware is split into two layers so that apps stay small.

PocketMageOS is the operating system. It owns boot, app switching, state, keyboard routing, and the screen dispatch loop. If you are changing how the device behaves, you are working in PocketMageOS.
PocketMage Library is the reusable hardware and UI support layer, shipped as the PocketMage SDK and vendored at Code/PocketMageOS/lib/PocketMage_SDK/. It wraps the display, storage, keyboard, audio, clock, and system helpers so apps never talk to hardware directly.

The split matters because both native apps and third-party ELF apps build on the same library. An app does three jobs - initialize, handle input, draw - and uses the library for everything else. Native apps are compiled into the firmware; ELF apps are built separately against the SDK and loaded from the SD card at runtime. The SDK is documented on its own SDK documentation site.

116.title: ELF Apps
116.text:
ELF Apps
Third-party apps are compiled outside the OS into a .app.elf, packed into a .tar with an overlay sidecar and an icon, and installed at runtime through the app loader. No firmware reflash is involved. This page covers the app from the OS side: how the loader runs it, where installed apps live, and what an app can rely on. The binary contract itself, the build tooling, and the full symbol surface are owned by the SDK documentation and are not duplicated here.
For building and shipping an app, start with the SDK docs:

App ABI - the binary contract
Overlay format - the .elfo sidecar
Building apps - the toolchain and make targets
Symbols - the host export surface

What an ELF app is
An ELF app is a standalone 32-bit ET_DYN program linked against the PocketMage SDK with PM_TARGET_APP. It links -nostdlib, so it ships no runtime of its own; everything it references, from malloc to the pm_* API, resolves from the host at load time.
The runner (src/elf_runner.cpp) loads an installed app in two stages. It reads the .app.elf from the SD card and relocates the base image with esp_elf, then loads the matching .elfo overlay sidecar, which pages the app’s code into executable RAM on demand and patches ISA-specific relocations. The entry (app_main) then runs in its own 16 KB task on core 1. While the app runs, the OS loop and the E-Ink task stand down and the app owns the UI through the host singletons.
Exiting is a return from app_main. No reboot is needed: the runner unloads the overlay, deinitializes the base image, and reopens HOME.
Packaging and installing

Build the app into <name>.app.elf and its <name>.elfo overlay sidecar.
Pack them with a 40x40 <name>_ICON.bin and an optional app.properties manifest into a plain .tar (make pack does this).
Copy the .tar onto the SD card, typically over USB.
Open the app loader on the device and use the swap action to install it into one of the four slots.

Installed apps live in /apps/slot1 through /apps/slot4 on the SD card and are tracked in NVS under ELFINFO1 through ELFINFO4. Launch an installed app from the home screen by typing A, B, C, or D, or from the loader.
The manifest (app.properties)
The loader reads an optional app.properties from the app’s slot directory (up to 1024 bytes). Recognized fields are name, version, author, and scope. The first three become the app’s display metadata and are passed to app_main as argv. scope (default all) restricts which pm_* symbols the app may resolve: anything outside its scope fails to resolve, so a mis-scoped app is rejected at load rather than reaching an API it did not declare. The runtime baseline (libc, libstdc++, ESP-IDF) stays available at any scope.
What an ELF app should assume

It runs without the native PocketMageOS app set. Do not call functions from src/OS_APPS/.
Keep the app self-contained and link against the SDK only.
Use the PocketMage library for hardware access, exactly like native apps.
The host exports a curated symbol set (generated into src/ELF_SYMS/esp_all_symbol.cpp), including pocketmage_sdk_version for version checks. A symbol outside that set must be added to the SDK surface before an app can resolve it.

127.text:
Making Apps
PocketMage apps come in two forms: native apps that ship inside PocketMageOS, and ELF apps that are sideloaded onto the device later. Native apps are the focus of this page; the full path for sideloaded apps is the ELF Apps guide.




  
  

Native appsCompiled into the OS and wired into the app dispatch switch.




  
  
  
  

ELF appsCompiled standalone, loaded from the SD card at runtime.




  
  

Native shapeNative apps are three functions: init, handle input, draw.


The basic app shape
Every PocketMage app has the same three jobs, and they map directly to three functions.

Initialize state - run once when the app opens. Set up whatever the app needs and mark the screen for a redraw.
Process keyboard input - run on every keypress. Read the key, update app state, and queue a redraw.
Draw the screen - run when the E-Ink needs to update. Render the current app state.

This pattern is visible in Code/PocketMageOS/include/globals.h (the prototypes) and in the app files under Code/PocketMageOS/src/OS_APPS/.
Start with the template
The app template is your starting point:

APP_TEMPLATE.cpp

It defines the three entry points a compiled-in app needs:
#include <globals.h>
#if PM_TARGET_APP
void APP_INIT() {
  // 1. set up app state
}

void processKB_APP() {
  // 2. handle a keypress
}

void einkHandler_APP() {
  // 3. draw the screen
}
#endif

Building the app step by step

Decide native vs ELF. If the app belongs to the device experience, make it native. If it is third-party or experimental, make it an ELF app so it can be installed and removed without reflashing the OS.
Pick the shared helpers. Browse the PocketMage Library before writing anything. Prompts (textPrompt()), file selection (fileWizardMini()), and timeouts (checkTimeout()) already exist; do not reimplement them.
Wire it into the OS (native only). Add an AppState entry, the three prototypes, and the switch cases marked // ADD APP CASES HERE in PocketMageV3.cpp. Then add a home-screen command if you want it launchable by name.
Test the keyboard path first. Get a keypress into your handler and onto the OLED before worrying about the E-Ink.
Test the E-Ink path second. Make sure drawing and refresh behave, including fast partial refreshes.
Check timeout, wake, and save last. Confirm the app resets the idle clock, handles sleep/wake without corrupting state, and saves before exit where it should.

Good app rules

Keep app state local and explicit; do not scatter globals.
Use shared helpers instead of duplicating them.
Keep draw code separate from input code.
Make exit, save, and sleep behavior obvious.
For native apps, follow the existing app in src/OS_APPS/ that does the closest job.

147.text:
App API Reference
Every PocketMage app, native or ELF, calls the same shared helpers. This page documents the exact names and what each one is for. Declarations live in Code/PocketMageOS/include/globals.h.
The two app styles

Native OS apps live in Code/PocketMageOS/src/OS_APPS/ and are wired into the dispatch switch.
ELF apps are built against the PocketMage SDK into a .app.elf and loaded by elf_runner at runtime. The APP_TEMPLATE.cpp scaffold shows the PM_TARGET_APP entry hooks.

Both call the same shared helpers below.
Compiled-in app entry points
A compiled-in third-party app implements three functions:
#include <globals.h>
#if PM_TARGET_APP
void APP_INIT() {
  // set up state; runs once when the app is entered
}

void processKB_APP() {
  // handle one keypress
}

void einkHandler_APP() {
  // draw the E-Ink screen
}
#endif

The PM_TARGET_APP build path is set by the SDK’s config.h, which selects the app entry hooks and excludes the OS app set. Standalone .app.elf apps enter through their own main instead.
Native OS app entry points
Native apps follow the same shape with app-specific names. Prototypes are declared in globals.h.

HOME_INIT() / processKB_HOME() / einkHandler_HOME()
TXT_INIT() / processKB_TXT_NEW() / einkHandler_TXT_NEW()
FILEWIZ_INIT() / processKB_FILEWIZ() / einkHandler_FILEWIZ()
SETTINGS_INIT() / processKB_SETTINGS() / einkHandler_SETTINGS()
TASKS_INIT() / processKB_TASKS() / einkHandler_TASKS()
CALENDAR_INIT() / processKB_CALENDAR() / einkHandler_CALENDAR()
JOURNAL_INIT() / processKB_JOURNAL() / einkHandler_JOURNAL()
LEXICON_INIT() / processKB_LEXICON() / einkHandler_LEXICON()
APPLOADER_INIT() / processKB_APPLOADER() / einkHandler_APPLOADER()
TERMINAL_INIT() / processKB_TERMINAL() / einkHandler_TERMINAL()

To add a native app, extend the AppState enum and add cases to the switch (CurrentAppState) in PocketMageV3.cpp, at the spots marked // ADD APP CASES HERE.
Dispatch helpers

processKB() - the main keyboard dispatch loop; routes a keypress to the active app
applicationEinkHandler() - the main screen dispatch; routes a refresh to the active app

App transitions

loadState(bool changeState = true, char bootKey = 0) - enter another app; runs its *_INIT()
wakeFromNowlater(char bootKey = 0) - restore the previous app state when waking
bootShortcutApp(char inchar) - maps a boot shortcut key to its app

Idle and timeout

checkTimeout() - check the idle timer and sleep if the timeout elapsed
resetIdle() - reset the idle clock so the app stays awake
disableTimeout - global flag; while set, the OS never sleeps

User input prompts

boolPrompt(promptText = "Are you sure?") - yes/no, returns 1 or 0

PocketMage Library
The PocketMage Library is the shared hardware, UI, and system layer the firmware links in-process. It lives in the PocketMage SDK, vendored at Code/PocketMageOS/lib/PocketMage_SDK/, and the same code is the contract external ELF apps build against. Reach for it when you want to talk to the screen, storage, keyboard, audio, clock, or other shared device systems without rewriting them in an app.
The SDK has its own reference documentation covering every module and the app-facing C ABI. This page is the firmware-side view: the same modules, as PocketMageOS code calls them.
Access pattern
Each hardware module is a singleton exposed as a function, so methods read CLASS().method():

Accessor
Use it for

Note the SD accessor is PM_SD(), not SD() - the fs::SD object is part of the Arduino filesystem API and is a different thing.
The umbrella header
Include pocketmage.h to pull in all the major feature modules plus the project config and shared assets. Inside PocketMageOS code, include globals.h first, which already pulls in the library.

Module map
PocketmageOLED
Drives the 256x32 OLED status display and on-screen system messages.

System State Reference
PocketMageOS is a state machine. The single CurrentAppState variable decides which app owns the keyboard and the screen at any moment. This page documents that state and everything around it: the enum, the home screen, boot shortcuts, and how dispatch works.
The AppState enum
CurrentAppState holds one value from AppState, declared in Code/PocketMageOS/include/globals.h:
enum AppState { HOME, TXT, FILEWIZ, USB_APP, COMM, SETTINGS, TASKS, CALENDAR, JOURNAL, LEXICON, APPLOADER, TERMINAL };




Value

How dispatch works
The OS has two dispatch functions in PocketMageV3.cpp:

processKB() - reads the keyboard and routes the keypress to the active app’s keyboard handler
applicationEinkHandler() - routes screen refresh to the active app’s draw handler

Both switch on CurrentAppState and call the matching per-app function. When you add a native app, you extend AppState and add cases in the spots marked // ADD APP CASES HERE.
The HOME state
The home screen has its own sub-state machine, HOMEState:
enum HOMEState { HOME_HOME, NOWLATER };


HOME_HOME - the normal home screen with the app grid
NOWLATER - the “save state” view that shows unsaved data before going to sleep

CurrentHOMEState tracks which one is active.

195.title: PocketMage Scripting Reference
195.text:
PocketMage Scripting Reference
This document details the Wrench script bindings available in the PocketMage OS. Functions are grouped by their operational category.

1. Input / Output & Terminal
print(text)
Appends a string to the terminal output buffer. Does not automatically refresh the screen.

Parameters: text (String) - The string to print.

Returns: None.

Example:
print("Hello, terminal!");



updateTerm()
Refreshes the terminal display to show the latest buffer contents.

Parameters: None.

Returns: None.

Example:
print("Loading...");
updateTerm();



prompt(promptText)
Opens a text input prompt interface and pauses script execution until the user submits or cancels.

Parameters: promptText (String) - The message displayed to the user.

Returns: (String) The entered text, or an empty string "" if the user cancels (_EXIT_).

Example:
name = prompt("Enter your name:");
print("Hello " + name);



boolPrompt(promptText)
Opens a yes/no boolean prompt interface.

Parameters: promptText (String) - The question displayed to the user.

Returns: (Int) 1 for yes/true, 0 for no/false.

Example:
if (boolPrompt("Save file?")) {
    writeFile("/data.txt", "saved");
}



timePrompt(defaultTime)
Opens a time selection interface.

Parameters: defaultTime (Int) - The initial time value to display.

Returns: (Int) The selected time.

Example:
alarm = timePrompt(1200);



datePrompt(defaultDate)
Opens a date selection interface.

Parameters: defaultDate (String) - The initial date to display (format: max 15 chars).

Returns: (String) The selected date.

Example:
dueDate = datePrompt("2026-05-01");



waitForKeypress(message)
Halts script execution and waits for the user to press a key.

Parameters: message (String) - Text to display while waiting.

Returns: None.

Example:
waitForKeypress("Press any key to continue...");




2. Main E-Paper Display
updateInk()
Pushes the current E-Ink drawing buffer to the physical e-paper display. This is a slow, blocking hardware update.

Parameters: None.

Returns: None.

Example:
inkText(10, 20, 2, 1, "Hello E-Ink");
updateInk();



inkBackground(color)
Fills the entire E-Ink screen with a solid color.

Parameters: color (Int) - 0 for white, 1 (or non-zero) for black.

Returns: None.

Example:
inkBackground(1);



inkRect(x, y, width, height, borderColor, fillColor)
Draws a rectangle on the E-Ink display buffer.

Parameters:

x, y (Int) - Origin coordinates.
width, height (Int) - Dimensions.
borderColor (Int) - 0 to draw border, 1 for no border.
fillColor (Int) - 0 to fill rectangle, 1 for transparent/no fill.


Returns: None.

Example:
inkRect(10, 10, 100, 50, 0, 1);



inkCircle(x, y, radius, borderColor, fillColor)
Draws a circle on the E-Ink display buffer.

Parameters:

x, y (Int) - Center coordinates.
radius (Int) - Radius in pixels.
borderColor (Int) - 0 to draw border, 1 for no border.
fillColor (Int) - 0 to fill circle, 1 for transparent/no fill.


Returns: None.

Example:
inkCircle(100, 100, 25, 0, 0);



inkText(x, y, size, color, text)
Renders text to the E-Ink display buffer.

Parameters:

x, y (Int) - Cursor start coordinates.
size (Int) - Font size mapping: 1 = 5x7 Fixed, 2 = 9pt Bold, 3 = 12pt Bold.
color (Int) - 0 for white text, 1 (or non-zero) for black text.
text (String) - Text to display.


Returns: None.

Example:
inkText(5, 50, 3, 1, "PocketMage");




3. Secondary OLED Display
updateOled()
Pushes the current OLED drawing buffer to the physical OLED screen and clears the internal buffer.

Parameters: None.

Returns: None.

Example:
oledText(0, 10, 2, 0, "OLED Active");
updateOled();



oledWord(text)
Abstracted wrapper to quickly print a formatted string directly to the OLED display.

Parameters: text (String) - Text to display.

Returns: None.

Example:
oledWord("Processing...");



sysMessage(msg, delayMs)
Flashes a high-priority system message on the OLED and blocks execution for the specified time.

Parameters:

msg (String) - System message text.
delayMs (Int) - Time in milliseconds to show the message before continuing.


Returns: None.

Example:
sysMessage("Script Error", 2000);



oledBackground(color)
Fills the OLED screen buffer.

Parameters: color (Int) - 0 to turn pixels ON, 1 to turn pixels OFF.

Returns: None.

Example:
oledBackground(1);



oledRect(x, y, width, height, borderColor, fillColor)
Draws a rectangle on the OLED buffer.

Parameters:

x, y (Int) - Origin coordinates.
width, height (Int) - Dimensions.
borderColor (Int) - 0 to draw border, 1 for no border.
fillColor (Int) - 0 to fill rectangle, 1 for transparent/no fill.


Returns: None.

Example:
oledRect(0, 0, 256, 32, 0, 1);



oledCircle(x, y, radius, borderColor)
Draws a circle outline on the OLED buffer. (No fill option supported).

Parameters:

x, y (Int) - Center coordinates.
radius (Int) - Radius in pixels.
borderColor (Int)

235.title: Scripting
235.text:
Scripting
The PocketMage TERMINAL app runs scripts written in Wrench, a lightweight C-like scripting language. Scripts can draw to the E-Ink and OLED displays, handle input, and talk to the rest of the system through the PocketMage library surface.
Wrench is a small interpreted language with a familiar if / while / var syntax. On PocketMage it is embedded inside the TERMINAL app, so every script is a .c file on the SD card that the terminal compiles and runs on demand.
What Wrench is for
Wrench sits one level above a native app. It trades raw performance for convenience:

Automation - script repeated terminal workflows instead of typing them each time
Custom screens - draw to the E-Ink or OLED with a few function calls
Prototyping - test an idea in a script before writing it as a native app
Device control - read the clock, battery, keyboard, and touch sensors from a script

Because scripts run in the TERMINAL app, they already have access to everything the terminal can reach: the displays, the SD card, prompts, and the shared system helpers.
Script lifecycle

Edit - create or open a .c script in TXT, or use the terminal’s editor. Save it to the SD card.
Compile - run brew <script>.c in the TERMINAL app to compile and execute it.
Run - the terminal interprets the script. print() sends output to the terminal buffer, updateTerm() paints it to the OLED.

The example scripts at the top of the page double as runnable tests: Basic Input/Output walks through the whole edit-to-run flow.
Bindings overview
Wrench bindings fall into five groups. The full command list documents every one with parameters, return values, and examples.

Input/output and terminal - print(), updateTerm(), prompt(), boolPrompt(), timePrompt(), datePrompt(), waitForKeypress()
E-Ink display - updateInk(), inkBackground(), inkRect(), inkCircle(), inkText()
OLED display - updateOled(), oledWord(), sysMessage(), oledBackground(), oledRect(), oledCircle(), oledText()
Hardware and system - getKey(), getTouch(), getBattery(), getBatteryVoltage(), setCpuSpeed(), sleep(), getTime(), getDate()
Filesystem - readFile(), writeFile()
General helpers - delay(), toInt(), random()

Language notes

Variables are declared with var and are dynamically typed. var x = "" creates a string; var i = 0 creates an integer.
Strings convert with toInt() where an integer is required.
Control flow uses C-style braces and parentheses.
random(min, max) returns a value in the inclusive range.
delay() is a blocking wait, in milliseconds.

Read this if

you want to automate something from the terminal app
you want to draw custom screens
you want to understand how Wrench fits into PocketMageOS

252.title: Format a MicroSD Card for PocketMage
252.text:
PocketMage SD Card Formatting Guide
These steps erase the card

This guide formats an SD card so PocketMage can mount it. The device reads a single FAT32 primary partition on an MBR partition table with 32 KB clusters; anything else is not detected reliably.
Supported SD card requirements

Card size: 2 GB to 32 GB microSD recommended. The slot accepts up to 2 TB, but cards above 32 GB must be forced to FAT32 and MBR and are not recommended.
Filesystem: FAT32
Partition scheme: MBR (Master Boot Record)
Partitions: a single primary partition
Cluster (allocation unit) size: 32 KB
Sector size: 512 bytes (default)

Not supported: exFAT, GPT partition tables, and 64 GB or larger cards unless you explicitly force FAT32 and MBR.
Windows (recommended)
Step 1: Open diskpart
Insert the card, open Command Prompt as Administrator, and run:
diskpart

Step 2: Identify the card
list disk

Find the disk number that matches your card size.
Select the correct disk

Step 3: Format the card (MBR + FAT32)
Replace X with your disk number, then run each line in the diskpart prompt:
select disk X
clean
convert mbr
create partition primary
format fs=fat32 unit=32k quick
assign
exit

Step 4: Verify (optional)
Open Disk Management, right-click the disk, and open Properties then Volumes. The partition style must read Master Boot Record (MBR).
macOS (Terminal, not Disk Utility)
Disk Utility often creates GPT layouts that do not work. Use the terminal.
Step 1: Identify the card
diskutil list

Find the disk number (for example, disk2).
Step 2: Erase and create MBR + FAT32
diskutil eraseDisk FAT32 PM_SD MBRFormat /dev/disk2

Step 3: Force 32 KB cluster size
sudo newfs_msdos -F 32 -c 64 /dev/disk2s1

-c 64 sets 64 sectors per cluster; at 512 bytes per sector that is a 32 KB cluster.
Step 4: Verify
diskutil info /dev/disk2 | grep "Partition Map"

The output must read Partition Map Scheme: Master Boot Record.
Linux
Step 1: Identify the card
lsblk

Example device: /dev/sdb.
Step 2: Remove existing partition data
sudo wipefs -a /dev/sdb

Step 3: Create the MBR partition table
sudo parted /dev/sdb --script mklabel msdos
sudo parted /dev/sdb --script mkpart primary fat32 1MiB 100%

Step 4: Format FAT32 with 32 KB clusters
sudo mkfs.fat -F 32 -s 64 /dev/sdb1

Step 5: Verify
lsblk -o NAME,SIZE,PTTYPE

PTTYPE must read dos.
Final checklist
Before using the card in PocketMage, confirm:

FAT32 filesystem
MBR partition table (not GPT)
one primary partition
32 KB cluster size
card size 32 GB or smaller

If any of these are wrong, the card may not be detected. If problems persist after following this guide, the card itself may be incompatible.
